The mallet heads are usually covered in leather or felt to shape the timbre. The complex stringing system needs precisely made metal parts to support it.

The pantalon is a very large struck dulcimer, classed as a chordophone, Hornbostel–Sachs 314.122. It is built with a double soundboard, about 2 metres long, and carries about 200 gut and metal strings, some doubled or tripled; as there are no dampers the strings ring on. It was invented by Pantaleon Hebenstreit in the early eighteenth century and named after him, and was used in French and German musical circles, where Hebenstreit and his pupils Maximilian Hellmann and Johann Baptist Gumpenhuber were almost the only virtuosos on it.
潘塔隆琴由Pantaleon Hebenstreit於十八世紀初發明，屬大型擊弦: The pantalon was invented by Pantaleon Hebenstreit in the early eighteenth century. It is a large struck dulcimer, Hornbostel–Sachs 314.122. It was briefly fashionable in French and German musical circles; Hebenstreit named it after himself and grew rich playing it. Few makers existed, and only Hebenstreit and his pupils Maximilian Hellmann and Johann Baptist Gumpenhuber were the leading performers. Its practice of letting the strings ring without dampers later turned into the pantalon damping device on early keyboard instruments.
潘塔隆琴的聆聽線索主要來自十八世紀法國與德國音樂圈，以及為演奏家 Maximil: The listening leads for the pantalon come mainly from eighteenth-century French and German musical circles, and from works written for the player Maximilian Hellmann. The source mentions three works by Caldara, eight by Johann Georg Reutter, and an aria by Johann Joseph Fux in Giunone placata (a theatrical celebration), which shows that it entered the vocal and theatrical scoring of the time. The actual performance occasions were above all the playing of Pantaleon Hebenstreit and his pupils.
潘塔隆琴音色明亮而富有光澤，具有如同古鋼琴般的清晰顆粒感，卻又帶有敲擊揚琴特有的: The pantalon's timbre is bright and glossy, with the clear articulation of a harpsichord and yet the warm resonance peculiar to a struck dulcimer. Its range is wide, from baritone to treble; the bass is steady and strong, the middle and upper register crystalline. Because the body is huge, its resonating cavity gives a thick, full sound and fills the space with layers of tone. Against the penetrating Italian dulcimer it is warmer; against the piano it has more of the immediacy and rhythmic drive of a percussion instrument. The many overtones of the vibrating strings give it a distinctive sheen, and in chamber music it can stand out without losing its elegance.
